did_you_know.text: Adullam was a town in the Shephelah, also mentioned in the story of David, who found refuge in a nearby cave. “The Adullamite” therefore probably identifies Hirah by his place of origin.
The duty of levirate marriage, or yibbum, appears here as a family responsibility to provide descendants for a brother who died childless. It is later stated explicitly as a law in Deuteronomy.
Sheep shearing was also a social and festive occasion, not merely farm work. In biblical stories, it often includes meals and gatherings.
The phrase “Petah Enayim” may be a place-name, but in Hebrew it also sounds like “opening of the eyes.” That is why translations interpret it in different ways.

A personal seal served in the ancient world as a form of identification and signature, especially on clay or documents. Together with the cord and staff, these objects could clearly identify their owner.
The word qedeshah is linguistically related to the word “holy,” but in this context it is usually understood as a woman associated with ritual sex. This is why translations vary.
The words “Recognize, please” echo the story of Joseph, where Judah and his brothers used the same phrase when showing Jacob Joseph’s robe. Here Judah must recognize objects that belong to him.
The scarlet thread is a narrative sign of identification: it marks the hand that appeared first, even though that baby did not ultimately emerge first.
The name Perez is connected with the Hebrew word for “breaking through.” According to the book of Ruth, Perez later becomes an ancestor of King David.
The name Zerah is probably connected with the idea of rising or shining. Thus the twins’ names reflect the circumstances of their birth and their appearance one after the other.
